answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
The GHGP electricity standard setting processes should be parallel and release a unified, coherent standard on a single date with public input on the interplay of the standards. A ton of carbon is a ton of carbon and, whenever possible, there should be one credible, consistent approach to measuring tons of carbon. A consequential standard could sit alongside the market-based and location-based methods and should apply to all emissions including induced and avoided emissions.

A standard that does not measure induced emissions is obviously inadequate for demand response and virtual power plants that shift the timing of demand. Temporal load shifting avoids emissions during some periods by inducing emissions in others and measures that ignore the induced emissions are neither credible nor useful. AMI aspires to be the right metric for such projects and can be if it includes induced emissions. Wind and solar projects induce emissions when grid operators keep additional fossil fueled generation online to deal with their variable output and these need to be considered, lest we unfairly disadvantage clean firm resources.

Consequential accounting offers a compelling intellectual framework that addresses many of the shortcomings in attributional systems. Indeed, many of the proposed revisions to the scope 2 attributional standards bring in concepts akin to consequential accounting. SSS, for example, is similar to additionality. Time and location matching attempt to ensure that consumption and generation have comparable emissions consequences. Consequential systems can measure additionality and emissions impacts more directly and precisely than the proposed Scope 2 attributional standard.

Electricity is an exceptionally data rich-field. Both the short-run and long-run emissions consequences of generation and consumption have been extensive studied both theoretically and empirically. The estimates are largely consistent. Economists have stood on decades of experience estimating counterfactuals and brought a variety of sophisticated, peer reviewed methods to that impact estimation. Greening electric grids is a fundamentally different challenge from preserving rain forests.

Harvard professor Bill Hogan reminds us that corporate energy decisions have marginal impacts in specific places and times, that can and should be precisely measured in “Scope 2: Physical Power Usage Accounting Is Fictional, Pricing And Marginal Impact Accounting Are Real.” We can address his important critique with consequential marginal operating and marginal build emissions rates. Here again, we can move toward a single, compelling GHG protocol that meshes with common grid management metrics rather than several incomparable ways to measure the same things that create unintended consequences.

AMI should offer credibility and comprehensiveness equivalent to the other scope 2 methods. If the consequential standard is optional and limited, while hourly matching is mandatory and universal, the consequential standard will likely be a largely irrelevant afterthought. Companies will be compared on and held to account for their comprehensive scope 2 numbers that every company reports. The case for a company to make a significant investment to report separately under AMI in such a scenario seems weak.

The public consultation on AMI offered a paucity of opportunities to comment on things like the relative role of the scope 2 and AMI standards and whether to synchronize their implementation. It instead focusses on implementation details for a fundamentally new standard. Please solicit more and broader feedback on AMI.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
A standard that does not measure induced emissions is obviously inadequate for demand response and virtual power plants that shift the timing of demand. Temporal load shifting avoids emissions during some periods by inducing emissions in others and measures that ignore the induced emissions are neither credible nor useful. AMI aspires to be the right metric for such projects and can be if it includes induced emissions. Wind and solar projects induce emissions when grid operators keep additional fossil fueled generation online to deal with their variable output and these need to be considered, lest we unfairly disadvantage clean firm resources.

The TWG Consequential subgroup recommended a formula that included induced emissions and 74% of the full TWG approved it. I am not alone in raising these concerns.
